summary:
AstroHealth is an autonomous, clinical-grade health monitoring system developed for astronauts on long-duration lunar and Martian transit missions. Addressing the NASA Space Apps Challenge, it enables crew members to independently detect, evaluate, and act upon physiological and psychological changes when communication latencies with Earth (up to 22 minutes) preclude real-time telemedicine.

The software tracks ten critical bio-indicators—including resting heart rate, blood pressure,

AstroHealth provides an interactive 7-zone anatomical body map with color-coded risk tiers, rapid vital logging with automated alert triage, dynamic time-series trend analytics, cumulative dosimeter tracking against NASA's 1,000 mSv career limit, and actionable countermeasure protocols (such as mandatory 2.5-hour ARED resistance exercise, bone-support nutrition, and circadian entrainment).

AstroHealth is essential because prolonged microgravity and cosmic radiation induce severe bone mineral loss, cardiovascular deconditioning, and immune dysregulation. By converting complex biometric telemetry into immediate, self-guided medical interventions without reliance on ground control, AstroHealth ensures crew health, operational autonomy, and mission success on journeys to Mars and beyond.

Project Details: AstroHealth

1. What does it do or how does it work?

AstroHealth is an autonomous, clinical-grade health monitoring and decision-support web application engineered specifically for astronauts on long-duration spaceflight missions (such as the Artemis lunar program and crewed Mars transits).

The system operates 100% locally within the spacecraft's onboard computing environment without relying on external cloud infrastructure. It continuously aggregates, evaluates, and contextualizes ten core physiological and behavioral indicators:

  • Cardiovascular & Pulmonary: Resting Heart Rate, Systolic Blood Pressure, Diastolic Blood Pressure, and Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO2\text{SpO}_2SpO2​).
  • Metabolic & Environmental: Core Body Temperature, Fasting Blood Glucose, and Daily Fluid Intake.
  • Neuro-Behavioral & Radiation: Daily Sleep Duration, Psychological Mood Score, and Daily Ionizing Radiation Dose.

AstroHealth processes these metrics through several interconnected modules:

  1. Interactive Anatomical Body Map (/bodymap): A custom vector-rendered human silhouette featuring seven interactive physiological zones (Head/Neuro, Cardiovascular, Metabolic, Blood Pressure site, Pulse Oximeter site, Musculoskeletal/Lower Body, and Collar Radiation Dosimeter). Each region dynamically changes color (Green = Nominal, Amber = Caution, Red = Critical) based on the worst-case status of its underlying indicators, allowing astronauts to tap any body area to inspect underlying physiological adaptations.
  2. Vital Signs Logging Console (/log): A high-efficiency input interface allowing astronauts to record vitals via keyboard, mouse, or touch. It performs instant clinical range validation, provides real-time action banners, and automatically dispatches abnormal readings to the mission alert queue.
  3. Dynamic Physiological Trends (/history): Powered by Recharts, this module provides time-series tracking across custom intervals (7 days, 14 days, 30 days, or All Time), rendering clinical threshold lines, moving averages, and automated statistical indicators (Min\text{Min}Min, Max\text{Max}Max, Avg\text{Avg}Avg, and trend vectors ↑,↓,→↑, ↓, →↑,↓,→).
  4. Clinical Countermeasure Directives (/guidance): A searchable medical formulary featuring dual-tab reference cards (Action Protocol and Pathophysiology) alongside standardized spaceflight directives for the 2.5-hour daily ARED exercise countermeasure, bone-demineralization nutritional protocols, circadian light entrainment, and emergency CAPCOM procedures.
  5. Space Hazards & Dosimeter Tracker (/hazards): Integrates live crew vitals directly with NASA's Five Hazards of Spaceflight and features a cumulative ionizing radiation meter tracking mission exposure against NASA's 1,000 mSv career limit.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Latency Autonomy: On missions to Mars, communication delays reach up to 22 minutes one-way (44-minute round-trip). AstroHealth provides instantaneous clinical triage, closing the telemedicine blackout gap.
  • Early Sub-Clinical Detection: Microgravity causes subtle, insidious physiological degradation (e.g., 1–2% monthly bone mineral loss, cephalad fluid redistribution, and cardiac deconditioning). AstroHealth's trend engine identifies multi-day anomalies before they manifest as acute clinical crises.
  • Bridges Data to Action: Unlike basic fitness trackers that merely report raw numbers, AstroHealth provides immediate, step-by-step medical countermeasures tailored to whether an indicator is low, high, or nominal, including explicit threshold criteria for when ground flight surgeons must be contacted.
  • Minimal Cognitive Overhead: Designed specifically for high-stress, sleep-deprived, or emergency operational conditions. Clean visual hierarchies and standardized color tiers prevent data misinterpretation.
  • Holistic Health Integration: Merges physical biometrics, environmental radiation doses, and psychological well-being into a single unified telemetry picture.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Ensuring Astronaut Survival on Deep Space Missions: By empowering astronauts to act as autonomous medical monitors and first responders, AstroHealth directly mitigates mission-abort risks caused by preventable medical events (e.g., renal stones from calcium dumping, severe orthostatic intolerance, or acute hypoxia).
  • Scalable Fleet Deployment: The lightweight, offline-first architecture can scale across diverse spaceflight environments—from small Orion capsules and the Lunar Gateway space station to pressurized Mars surface rovers and planetary base camps.
  • Terrestrial Telemedicine Spin-offs: The exact same software architecture directly benefits remote, isolated environments on Earth where traditional medical access is unavailable—such as Antarctic winter-over research stations, deep-sea exploration vessels, remote mining outposts, and rural disaster-relief clinics.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3.
  • Framework & Core Engine: Next.js 16 (React 19, Turbopack, App Router).
  • Data Visualization: Recharts for responsive, SVG-based clinical time-series telemetry charts.
  • Styling & Design System: Tailwind CSS v4, utilizing a customized dark zinc aerospace palette and standardized NASA medical status color tokens.
  • State Management & Storage: React Context API + useReducer with automatic local storage synchronization, ensuring 100% offline data persistence without cloud requirements.
  • Version Control & Hosting: Git, GitHub repository (https://github.com/MohAymann/Nasa.git).
  • Hardware Compatibility: Fully responsive across spacecraft avionics touchscreens, ruggedized crew tablets (e.g., iPad/Surface), laptop workstations, and heads-up displays.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Interactive Anatomical Symptom Correlator: Instead of overwhelming crew members with tables of detached laboratory numbers, AstroHealth maps biometrics onto an interactive, vector-drawn anatomical body map. If an astronaut feels lower limb fatigue or upper-body pressure, tapping that region immediately links their physical symptom to fluid shift dynamics, ARED exercise targets, and blood pressure telemetry.
  • "Why + How" Dual-Layer Clinical Guidance: Most medical dashboards tell users what a number is; AstroHealth explains why the space environment caused it (spaceflight pathophysiology) and how to counteract it (concrete operational checklists).
  • Integrated Radiation Career Dosimeter: Innovatively combines daily semiconductor dosimeter logging with long-term radiation career thresholds, visualizing ionizing cosmic ray risks in a way that is easily interpretable during routine flight ops.
  • Purpose-Driven Aerospace Minimalism: We intentionally avoided gimmicky, unscientific design tropes (such as purple neon glows and decorative floating particles) in favor of a sleek, flight-deck-grade console inspired by NASA Orion display standards and human-system integration guidelines (NASA-STD-3001).

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • NASA Human Research Program (HRP) 5 Hazards: Mapped our features directly against Space Radiation, Isolation and Confinement, Altered Gravity, Distance from Earth, and Hostile Closed Environments.
  • Microgravity Physiological Adaptations: We accounted for the cephalad fluid shift ("puffy face syndrome"), decreased plasma volume, blunted baroreceptor sensitivity, trabecular bone loss, insulin resistance, and circadian disruption from 16 daily orbital sunsets.
  • Human Factors and Ergonomics (NASA-STD-3001): Designed high-contrast UI elements for dim cabin lighting, oversized touch targets for microgravity float interactions or gloved hands, and rapid keyboard entry for quick routine check-ins.
  • Complete Offline Independence: Factored in deep-space comm blackouts by ensuring the application runs entirely client-side with zero external API or cloud server dependencies.
